In the 19th century, the chief competition to the *Times* was the *[Los Angeles Examiner](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Herald_Examiner "Los Angeles Herald Examiner")* followed by the smaller *[Los Angeles Tribune](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Tribune_(1886%E2%80%931890) "Los Angeles Tribune (1886–1890)").* In December 1903, newspaper magnate [William Randolph Hearst](/wiki/William_Randolph_Hearst "William Randolph Hearst") began publishing the *Los Angeles Examiner* as a direct morning competitor to the *Times.*[[118]](#cite_note-118) In the 20th century, the *[Los Angeles Express](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Herald-Examiner "Los Angeles Herald-Examiner")*, [Manchester Boddy](/wiki/Manchester_Boddy "Manchester Boddy")'s [Los Angeles *Daily News*](/wiki/Illustrated_Daily_News "Illustrated Daily News"), a Democratic newspaper, were both afternoon competitors.[[119]](#cite_note-RedInk-119)

By the mid-1940s, the *Times* was the leading newspaper in terms of circulation in the [Greater Los Angeles](/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles"). In 1948, it launched the *Los Angeles Mirror*, an afternoon tabloid, to compete with both the *Daily News* and the merged *Herald-Express*. In 1954, the *Mirror* absorbed the *Daily News*. The combined paper, the *Mirror-News*, ceased publication in 1962, when the Hearst afternoon *[Herald-Express](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Herald_Examiner "Los Angeles Herald Examiner")* and the morning *[Los Angeles Examiner](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Examiner "Los Angeles Examiner")* merged to become the *[Herald-Examiner](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Herald-Examiner "Los Angeles Herald-Examiner")*.[[120]](#cite_note-Pitt-120) The *Herald-Examiner* published its last number in 1989.

In 2014, the *Los Angeles Register*, published by Freedom Communications, then-parent company of the *[Orange County Register](/wiki/Orange_County_Register "Orange County Register")*, was launched as a daily newspaper to compete with the *Times*. By late September of that year, however, the *Los Angeles Register* closed.[[121]](#cite_note-121)[[122]](#cite_note-122)

Earth and Venus have a near [orbital resonance](/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance") of 13:8 (Earth orbits eight times for every 13 orbits of Venus).[[161]](#cite_note-163)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Britain-fractal-coastline-50km.png/250px-Britain-fractal-coastline-50km.png)](/wiki/File:Britain-fractal-coastline-50km.png)

An example of the [coastline paradox](/wiki/Coastline_paradox "Coastline paradox"). If measured using an interval of 125 mi (200 km), the coast of Great Britain has a length of about 1,500 mi (2,400 km). Using an interval of 30 mi (50 km), the length is about 2,100 mi (3,400 km).

The [coastline paradox](/wiki/Coastline_paradox "Coastline paradox") states that a coastline does not have a well-defined length. Measurements of the [length of a coastline](/wiki/How_Long_Is_the_Coast_of_Britain%3F_Statistical_Self-Similarity_and_Fractional_Dimension "How Long Is the Coast of Britain? Statistical Self-Similarity and Fractional Dimension") behave like a [fractal](/wiki/Fractal "Fractal"), being different at different scale intervals (distance between points on the coastline at which measurements are taken). The smaller the scale interval (meaning the more detailed the measurement), the longer the coastline will be.[[a]](#cite_note-1) This "magnifying" effect is greater for convoluted coastlines than for relatively smooth ones.

Development on a tenth main *Fast & Furious* film began by October 2020, with Lin returning to direct. The film's official title was revealed when [principal photography](/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began in April 2022. Lin left as director later that month, citing creative differences, though he retained writing and producing credits. Leterrier was then hired as his replacement a week later and performed several [uncredited rewrites](/wiki/Script_doctor "Script doctor") to the screenplay. Longtime franchise composer [Brian Tyler](/wiki/Brian_Tyler "Brian Tyler") returned to score the film. With an estimated net production budget of $378.8 million, *Fast X* is the [sixth-most expensive film ever made](/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#Most_expensive_productions_(unadjusted_for_inflation) "List of most expensive films"). Filming lasted until that August, taking place in London, Rome, Turin, Lisbon, and Los Angeles.

*Fast X* premiered in Rome on May 12, 2023, and was released in the United States on May 19, by [Universal Pictures](/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures"). The film received mixed reviews from critics, with praise for its action sequences and Momoa's performance but criticism towards the writing, and grossed $714 million worldwide, failed to [breakeven](/wiki/Box-office_bomb "Box-office bomb") despite becoming the [fifth-highest-grossing film of 2023](/wiki/2023_in_film "2023 in film").[[3]](#cite_note-Reid-4) A sequel, titled *Fast Forever*, is scheduled to be released on March 17, 2028.

After World War II left Europe in ruins, Brazil hosted the [1950 FIFA World Cup](/wiki/1950_FIFA_World_Cup "1950 FIFA World Cup") unopposed.

At the tournament's group stage, Brazil defeated [Mexico](/wiki/Mexico_national_football_team "Mexico national football team") 4–0 at the [Maracanã](/wiki/Maracan%C3%A3_Stadium "Maracanã Stadium") in [Rio de Janeiro](/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") (then the Brazilian capital), tied with [Switzerland](/wiki/Switzerland_national_football_team "Switzerland national football team") 2–2 at the [Pacaembu](/wiki/Pacaembu_Stadium "Pacaembu Stadium") in [São Paulo](/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo "São Paulo"), and returned to the Maracanã to defeat [Yugoslavia](/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team "Yugoslavia national football team") 2–0.

Unlike the other tournaments before and after, this edition had a final group stage to decide the champions. At this stage, Brazil defeated [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden_men%27s_national_football_team "Sweden men's national football team") 7-1 and [Spain](/wiki/Spain_national_football_team "Spain national football team") 6–1, both at the Maracanã.

The team went into the last game of the final round, against [Uruguay](/wiki/Uruguay_national_football_team "Uruguay national football team") at the Maracanã needing only a draw to win the World Cup. Brazil opened the score, but Uruguay made a comeback and won the match 2–1 with a goal by [Alcides Ghiggia](/wiki/Alcides_Ghiggia "Alcides Ghiggia") deciding the match, and Uruguay won the World Cup in a game known as the [Maracanazo](/wiki/Uruguay_v_Brazil_(1950_FIFA_World_Cup) "Uruguay v Brazil (1950 FIFA World Cup)"). The Nationals' reign as defending champions ended with a 109–104 loss in [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). After the season, the team dropped gold from their uniforms, wearing just red and blue for the remainder of their tenure.

The Nationals got off to a slow start as coach Cervi was fired and replaced by [Paul Seymour](/wiki/Paul_Seymour_(basketball) "Paul Seymour (basketball)"). In the playoffs, the Nationals had trouble knocking off the defending champion Warriors but advanced to the Eastern Finals with two straight wins. The Nationals were swept in three games by the eventual champions, the Celtics.

Fort Wayne and Rochester had moved on to Detroit and Cincinnati for the [1957–58 season](/wiki/1957%E2%80%9358_NBA_season "1957–58 NBA season"), leaving the Syracuse Nationals as the last small-town team in the big city NBA. Regardless, they still finished in second place with a 41–31 record. In the playoffs, the Nationals fell in the first round as they lost a three-game series to the Philadelphia Warriors.

Despite a mediocre 35–37 record for the [1958–59 season](/wiki/1958%E2%80%9359_NBA_season "1958–59 NBA season") the Nationals made the playoffs again by finishing in third place.
